rationale: A wins because it keeps four real stories in separate lanes: IPO-watch disclosure, open-vs-closed vendor conflict, regulated-buyer custody, and open-model economics. Its headline "Databricks discloses a $3B run rate while signaling an IPO it won't put a date on" is grounded and journalist-shaped; B's "Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit. Databricks says it has one." invents auditability the update did not provide. B has bones, but it decorates too many gaps instead of labeling them as gaps.
gaps_in_A: "For banks and hospitals, the AI question is custody, not capability" is a strong lens, but "banks and hospitals" are inferred examples, not supplied facts. Fine as a target beat, dangerous as a factual claim without a customer.

"an enterprise that cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API" overstates the update. The source says regulated enterprises are the target and fine-tuning on own data is the pitch; it does not prove they categorically cannot use third-party APIs.
"Databricks gives its model away" is a little too cute before the license is examined. An "open license" can still carry restrictions, which A correctly flags later but muddies in the headline.

A misses one useful accountability wrapper around self-reported model benchmarks plus private-company financial disclosure. It handles the proof needs, but it could have made that provenance question its own sharper angle.
gaps_in_B: "models they can audit. Databricks says it has one" is invented. Open licensing and fine-tuning do not automatically mean auditability, audit logs, or compliance-grade inspection.
"$3B ARR" is sloppy. The update says "$3B in annualized revenue"; ARR may be the right term, but the whole point is to clarify what the company means before repeating it as fact.

"unaudited" in "Databricks claims $3B ARR and 60% growth — unaudited" asserts more than the update gives. Privately held and self-reported is enough; don't add a legal/accounting claim you can't prove.

"government IT," "data residency," and "audit logging" import regulatory requirements that are plausible but not in the update. That is how a good angle gets a reporter to ask, "Where did you get that?"
